### What the trailing candidate needs

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(page.needs_table())
```

*Had* is the trailing candidate's share of the two leading candidates' votes on election night; *needs* is the share
of their special votes that would overturn the election-night margin, at the expected number of special votes;
*forecast* is the share the model expects. Each seat's special votes are best compared with its own ordinary votes. In the chart, the grey shapes are how much more
{{< var specials.second >}} each seat's special votes were than its ordinary votes at past elections. The black bar
is this year's forecast (thick: 50%, thin: 90%), and the tinted zone is where the trailing candidate overtakes.

## How the forecast works {#method}

The official result is the election-night count, plus the official count's change to the ordinary votes, plus
the special votes. Each part is forecast from the Electoral Commission's results by voting place for these seats
at the `{python} f.get("years", "–")` elections (`{python} f.get("n_cases", "–")` seat-elections), and each
simulation draws all three.

**How many special votes.** A seat's special votes per ordinary vote are stable from one election to the next
relative to the country's: `{python} f.get("most_specials", "–")` has had about `{python} f.get("most_ratio", "–")`
per 100 ordinary votes, `{python} f.get("fewest_specials", "–")` about `{python} f.get("fewest_ratio", "–")`. The
model learns each seat's level and moves it with the national figure. The Commission estimates `{python} f.get("estimate", "–")` special votes still to
count; its election-night estimates have fallen short of the final count by 5 to 6% (2020 and 2023), so the model
expects about `{python} f.get("final_specials", "–")`. That is `{python} f.get("ratio", "–")`% as many per
ordinary vote as in 2023.

**How the special votes split.** Each seat's special votes are modelled as a shift from its own ordinary votes,
on the log-ratio scale against {{< var specials.first >}}’s candidate:

$$
\eta_{s,c} = x_s + \mu_c + \alpha + \gamma_c + \beta_s + \varepsilon_{s,c}
$$

where $x_s$ is the seat's election-night vote, $\mu_c$ the average shift of overseas or domestic special votes,
$\alpha$ this election's national shift, $\gamma_c$ how far overseas and domestic votes part ways in it, $\beta_s$
the seat's own lasting difference and $\varepsilon_{s,c}$ the rest. Special votes are then drawn from a multinomial
distribution with shares $\operatorname{softmax}(0, \eta_{s,c})$. Fitted to past elections, the national shift of
domestic special votes towards {{< var specials.second >}}’s candidate was `{python} f.get("past", "–")` points in an
evenly split seat. This year's is a fresh draw from that spread, with Student-t tails because three elections cannot
bound it: `{python} f.get("shift_med", "–")` points (90% interval `{python} f.get("shift_lo", "–")` to
`{python} f.get("shift_hi", "–")`).

**The 2025 enrolment change.** The Electoral Amendment Act 2025 closed enrolment 13 days before election day, so
nobody could enrol while voting. Those voters used to cast special votes in New Zealand; the national figures imply
about `{python} f.get("removed", "–")`% of the domestic special votes are gone. They are mostly young and recently
moved, so the model assumes, as an editorial judgement, that they leaned away from {{< var specials.first >}}
compared with the special votes that remain. That moves the domestic special votes about
`{python} f.get("enrol_pp", "–")` points towards {{< var specials.first >}} (90%: `{python} f.get("enrol_lo", "–")`
to `{python} f.get("enrol_hi", "–")`). The assumption is in
[`config/specials.yml`](https://github.com/ariedotcodotnz/nz-poll-of-polls/blob/main/config/specials.yml).

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(page.official_count_text())
```

All parameters are estimated together with the NUTS sampler in [NumPyro](https://num.pyro.ai), and every simulation
draws one set of them, one national shift shared by all the seats, then each seat's volume, split and recheck.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(page.official_count_table())
```

## How well it has worked

Each past election was forecast with the model refitted on the other two, starting from the election-night count
(2017, 2023) or from the official ordinary votes where the election-night count was not archived (2020). Three rules
of thumb get the same expected number of special votes. CRPS is the average error of the whole forecast
distribution, in votes of final margin; lower is better.

```{python}
#| output: asis
print(page.backtest_table())
```
